title: Tony Gilroy's Behemoth! review: Pedro Pascal drama hits wrong notes
content:
Tony Gilroy, known for directing the Bourne films and the Star Wars spin-off Andor, has released his first feature film since 2012’s The Bourne Legacy, a classical music drama titled Behemoth!. The film features a score by a group of nine A-list composers known as The Behemoth! Collective and stars Pedro Pascal as a womanizing central character. The review describes the movie as a forgettable production marred by stylistic gimmicks, noting that Pascal stumbles through the role.

Gilroy previously directed Tilda Swinton to an Oscar for her performance in the legal drama Michael Clayton. Critics had anticipated that Behemoth! would be an intriguing return for the director, who is recognized for balancing slick action with deeply felt drama. However, the new film is characterized as hitting the wrong notes despite its stacked cast and high-profile musical lineup.
summary: Tony Gilroy's new classical music drama Behemoth! features a stacked cast and a score from nine A-list composers. The film is criticized for being forgettable and marred by stylistic gimmicks.
author: Guardian Culture

title: New York production re-stages 1993 Larry Kramer and Anthony Fauci C-SPAN debate
content:
A New York production is re-staging a 1993 televised debate between Aids activist Larry Kramer and Anthony Fauci, then director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases. The original confrontation took place on November 30, 1993, on C-Span, a cable channel typically associated with congressional coverage rather than the high-intensity verbal exchanges seen on programs like CNN’s Crossfire. During the hour-long discussion, moderated by journalist Steve Scully, the two men clashed over the US government’s response to the Aids crisis, with Fauci asserting institutional legitimacy and Kramer arguing that institutions presiding over genocide lack it.

Scully attempted to keep the conversation focused on centrist concerns, primarily regarding money, while redirecting the pair when passions erupted. The broadcast also featured phone calls from civilians whose empathy and expertise in Aids varied widely. Although the segment was described as an exhausting hour that settled little, it demonstrated the dynamic of people yelling at each other loudly enough to be heard while also listening. The new production aims to bring this "extraordinary hour" to life as a masterclass of controlled fury.
summary: A New York production re-stages the 1993 C-SPAN debate between Aids activist Larry Kramer and Anthony Fauci, director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases. The event featured journalist Steve Scully moderating the two men as they argued about the US government's response to the Aids crisis.
author: Guardian Culture

title: ‘Brave from the beginning’: 20 years of Friday Night Lights – the sports drama that dared to be different
content:
The sports drama Friday Night Lights marked its 20th anniversary, having launched the careers of Jesse Plemons and Michael B. Jordan while allowing its cast to improvise in a fresh manner. The series, set in small-town Texas, depicted the intense cultural significance of high school football in communities where the outcome of Friday night games defined the local mood for days.

Britt Daniel, the frontman of the Texas band Spoon, noted the show’s authenticity by comparing its setting to his hometown of Temple, which he described as very similar to the fictional town of Odessa. Daniel recalled that in such towns, everything centered around the Friday football game, and he experienced significant social tension and physical threats during his youth. He stated that residents had to look over their shoulder in public spaces like malls, parking lots, and parties because people were eager to fight.
summary: It launched the careers of Jesse Plemons and Michael B Jordan, and let its stars improvise in a way that was fresh and new. This show about smalltown US football was confident, trailblazing – and wonderfulI’ve been around the south of the US enough to have seen the importance of football: little burgs where the high-school football field has stands that wouldn’t disgrace a League Two soccer club in the UK.

title: Lamine Yamal stars again as Spain see off Czechia and maintain perfect start
content:
Spain secured a 3‑1 victory over Czechia in Oviedo, extending their perfect start to the Nations League and keeping them a single point from the quarter‑finals. Teenager Lamine Yamal opened the scoring within six minutes, marking the third consecutive game in which he netted early. The goal, described by Spain’s manager Luis de la Fuente as a sign that Yamal is “on course to become a legend,” helped Spain complete their World Cup homecoming.

After a 2‑0 halftime lead—thanks to a second goal from Rodrigo Hernández—Spain substituted Yamal. Czechia, however, rallied in the second half, with Jiri Slama scoring on 69 minutes. In the 79th minute, a potential equaliser from Ryan Naderi was ruled out by referee Vassilis Fotias for a foul on Robin Le Normand, as the free‑kick that led to the attempt was swung in. Spain’s win leaves them a point away from the Nations League quarter‑finals.
summary: Lamine Yamal scored twice in Spain's 3-1 win over Czechia in Oviedo, keeping Spain a point from the Nations League quarter finals. Spain's manager Luis de la Fuente praised Yamal as a future legend, while Czechia's late comeback attempt was denied by referee Vassilis Fotias.

title: Bowie gets Pocognoli off mark with Scotland victory in North Macedonia
content:

John McGinn added a 22nd international goal from the penalty spot, while Scott McKenna was sent off late in the game. The result left the scoreline reflecting Scotland’s dominance, though a late dismissal and a failure to score more than five goals could have irritated Pocognoli.

The win keeps Scotland alive and kicking in section B1 of the Nations League, though the team will face far stiffer challenges in future fixtures.

The judge emphasized that “freedom from persistent, dragnet‑style surveillance while in public is not a foreign concept in our society, and it is a reasonable expectation that society…”  

The decision highlights the need for probable cause before accessing AI‑derived video data.
summary: An Oklahoma federal judge ruled on Friday that warrantless searches using AI‑powered surveillance camera data, such as that collected by Flock Safety’s technology, may violate the Fourth Amendment without adequate probable cause. title: KAIST study finds group security boosts detail and persuasiveness of dissent
content:
A research team at KAIST has found that members who feel securely accepted within a group are able to voice dissenting opinions more persuasively and in greater detail. The study suggests that such secure environments also make other members more receptive to incorporating dissenting views into decision‑making.

The researchers note that when every participant in a meeting echoes the same opinion, organizations risk overlooking warning signs and missing new ideas. By fostering a sense of security, groups can encourage richer dissent that improves the quality of collective judgments.
summary: A research team from KAIST says that when members feel securely accepted in a group, they can express dissenting opinions in greater detail and more persuasively. The study adds that other members may be more willing to use those dissenting views in decision‑making, and uniform agreement can cause organizations to miss warning signs and new ideas.

title: Human tau seeds trigger disease-specific shapes in mouse brains
content:
A new study reveals that human tau seeds induce disease-specific shapes within mouse brains. Tau is a protein naturally present in the brain, where it plays an essential role in proper neuron development and facilitates communication between neurons.

When this protein becomes misshapen or misfolded, it can drive the progression of neurodegenerative diseases. The abnormal buildup of tau is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, and scientists have also linked misfolded tau to more than 20 other neurodegenerative conditions.

content:

While the mechanism of this momentum exchange is not a new concept, researchers are investigating the specific effects that occur under conditions of long-term global warming.
summary: Atmospheric circulation carries angular momentum and can exchange it with the solid Earth to slightly alter the planet's rotation rate. The article investigates how this process occurs under long-term global warming.

title: Physicists Find Topological Wave Knots in Materials That Resist Imperfections
content: Physicists have identified topological properties in certain materials and devices, characterized by wave behaviors that resemble knots in a rope. These properties are defined by whole numbers that remain unchanged despite small imperfections, much like a knot persists through stretching or twisting until the rope is cut. This robustness against defects and noise has established topology as a central concept in modern physics, offering potential for the development of resilient electronics, photonics, and quantum devices.
summary: Physicists have found that some materials and devices carry topological properties in how waves move through them. These properties, labeled by whole numbers that do not change under small imperfections, promise electronics, photonics, and quantum devices that tolerate defects and noise.

The incident mirrors recent execution failures in other states, where inmates and their legal representatives have argued in court that such errors constitute cruel and unusual punishment.
summary: Tennessee's botched execution of Christa Pike is renewing scrutiny over how states carry out the death penalty. The attempt mirrors recent failures in other states where inmates and lawyers argue such errors amount to cruel punishment.
author: The Hill

title: Greens to Offer Two-Year Jobs to Unemployed Under-24s
content: Mothin Ali, the co-deputy leader of the Greens, announced at the party’s conference that the party intends to offer two-year jobs to unemployed individuals under the age of 24. Ali stated that many young people are currently "bored, desperate and lost."
summary: The Greens plan to offer two-year jobs to unemployed people under 24. Co-deputy leader Mothin Ali told the party's conference that many young people are "bored, desperate and lost".
author: BBC Politics

title: New Study Finds Unknown Brain Circuit Linked to OCD
content:
Treatment for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), a mental health condition defined by distressing, uncontrollable thoughts and repetitive behaviors, has traditionally relied on psychotherapy and medication to manage symptoms. New research has identified a previously unknown brain circuit involved in the condition.

This discovery could serve as a key step toward developing treatments that target specific brain regions, potentially allowing for better control of OCD.
summary: A study has identified a previously unknown brain circuit involved in obsessive‑compulsive disorder. This discovery could lead to treatments that target specific brain regions to better control the condition.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Menopause is a major health milestone, yet health records barely track it—new research
content:
A recent study has highlighted that menopause, a major health milestone for anyone with ovaries who lives long enough, is rarely documented in medical records.  

The research notes that menopause is a natural transition in midlife that can strongly affect a person's quality of life and increase their current and future risk of heart disease, osteoporosis, and other health issues.  

Given these significant health implications, it is notable that whether someone is experiencing or has gone through menopause is seldom recorded in their medical records.
summary: Anyone with ovaries who lives long enough will experience menopause. Medical records do not consistently reflect whether a person is experiencing or has gone through menopause, despite its impact on quality of life and risk of heart disease, osteoporosis, and other issues.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Injectable Foam Prototype Could Seal Deep Wounds and Prevent Amputations
content:
Injectable foam prototype could seal deep wounds and help prevent amputations

A new prototype uses a caulking gun filled with silicone compound to allow doctors and nurses to seal deep wounds caused by blast injuries. The device is intended for future use in clinical settings.

By sealing such wounds, the technology aims to prevent amputations and reduce mortality among patients with severe injuries.
summary: A caulking gun filled with silicone compound will allow doctors and nurses to seal deep blast‑injury wounds. This could prevent amputations and reduce mortality for patients with severe wounds.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Brain scans show shared changes during depression treatment and distinct antidepressant effects
content:
Brain scans have revealed that while depression treatment triggers common changes in the brain, some patients experience distinct antidepressant effects, according to new research. The study highlights how neuroimaging can capture both shared and individualized responses to therapy.

Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a widespread mental health condition primarily marked by persistent low mood or loss of interest in daily activities. It remains a significant challenge for patients and clinicians alike.

Although several medications are available to treat depression, identifying the right one for each individual can take time, underscoring the need for personalized approaches to treatment.
summary: Brain scans reveal shared neural changes during depression treatment and distinct effects of antidepressants in some patients. Major depressive disorder is a common mental health condition characterized by persistent low mood or loss of interest, and finding an effective medication can take time.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Climate change harms Indigenous children's health worldwide, study of 53 reports
content:
A review of 53 studies has found that climate change is affecting the health of Indigenous children worldwide. The research indicates that these children are experiencing significant climate‑related health impacts.  

The study reports a range of effects, including malnutrition, infectious diseases, impacts on mental health and cultural well‑being, and problems before birth.
summary: Indigenous children across the globe are experiencing significant climate-related health impacts. These impacts include malnutrition, infectious diseases, mental health and cultural well-being effects, and problems before birth, according to a new study.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Salinas, Steinbeck's hometown, ranks as US's least affordable city for middle class
content:
A recent Brookings Institution analysis found that John Steinbeck’s hometown of Salinas is the least affordable city in the United States for the middle class.

Nestled between two mountain ranges at the crook of central California’s coastline, the Salinas Valley is known as the “salad bowl of the world.” Farm workers stoop over neatly lined rows of crops off Highway 101 to harvest more than half of the nation’s supply of lettuce and nearly a third of its strawberries.

The valley’s rich soil inspired Steinbeck to portray it as a promised land in his literary depictions of people chasing the American dream—immigrants, farm workers, and westward‑moving hopefuls hungering for a better life.
summary: A Brookings Institution analysis found that Salinas, John Steinbeck’s hometown, is the least affordable city in the US for the middle class. The valley, known as the “salad bowl of the world,” produces more than half of the nation’s lettuce and nearly a third of its strawberries, and Steinbeck used it as the promised land in his depictions of people chasing the American dream.
author: Guardian Business

title: French court study shows national courts key to deportation decisions
content:
French court rulings on deportation illustrate how judges balance conflicting rules on forced removal. A new study, published in the International Journal of Migration and Border Studies, examines the complex legal framework that governs European deportation practices.

The paper notes that European, national, and human‑rights law all intersect in deportation cases. The author argues that this web of regulations shapes how decisions are made in France.

Based on analysis of 100,000 French court cases, the study finds that national courts play a central role in deciding whether individuals can be removed.
summary: A study published in the International Journal of Migration and Border Studies analyzes 100,000 French court cases. It shows that judges navigate conflicting European, national and human rights rules, with national courts playing a central role in removal decisions.
author: Phys.org

title: Energy production, virus defenses and toxin loading identified as bacterial vulnerabilities
content:
Antimicrobial resistance is recognized as one of the world’s leading public‑health threats. The condition, often described as a silent pandemic, has already caused millions of deaths each year.  

According to estimates from the World Health Organization, if antimicrobial‑resistant bacteria are not contained, the number of deaths could rise to 10 million annually by 2050.  

These projections underscore the urgent need for continued surveillance and new strategies to combat resistant bacterial infections.
summary: Energy production, virus defenses and toxin loading have been identified as vulnerabilities in antimicrobial‑resistant bacteria. Antimicrobial resistance is a top global public‑health threat that currently causes millions of deaths annually and could reach 10 million deaths per year by 2050, according to WHO estimates.
author: Phys.org

title: Interactive Tool Reveals State-by-State Private Equity Health Care Investments
content:
New interactive tool tracks private equity investments in health care across U.S.

A new interactive tool was launched on Tuesday, Sept. 8, giving policymakers, researchers, journalists and the public a state‑by‑state view of private equity investments in U.S. health care.

The tool allows users to examine how private equity is shaping the health care sector across individual states.
summary: A new interactive tool was launched on Tuesday, Sept. 8. It provides a state-by-state view of private equity investments in U.S. health care for policymakers, researchers, journalists, and the public.
author: Phys.org

title: Milky Way may have begun as thousands of galaxies, new simulations suggest
content:
Milky Way may have begun as thousands of galaxies, new simulations suggest

In the early days of the universe, our home looked very different from how it does today. Back then, the region in our universe that would eventually become our Milky Way neighborhood was a collection of thousands of smaller galaxies—some pumping out tons of new stars, others filled only with gas or littered with dead stars and black holes.
summary: New simulations indicate that the region that would become the Milky Way was once a collection of thousands of smaller galaxies. These galaxies varied, with some forming many new stars, while others contained only gas or were filled with dead stars and black holes.
author: Phys.org

title: Short Breath Extends Mating Calls of Male Tokay Geckos
content:
A short breath extends the mating calls of male tokay geckos

Tokay geckos (Gekko gecko) are large, mostly nocturnal reptiles native to parts of Asia. They are among the few non‑bird reptiles that produce sounds to attract potential mates, defend their territory and signal distress.

Male tokay geckos’ calls typically begin with quieter rattles, followed by louder two‑part sounds that can sound like “ge‑ko” or “to‑kay.” These vocalizations help the males attract mates, defend territory, and signal distress.
summary: Male tokay geckos (Gekko gecko) use mating calls that start with quieter rattles and finish with louder two‑part sounds. A short breath extends these calls, aiding in mate attraction, territorial defense, and distress signaling.
author: Phys.org

title: Scientists find hundreds of hair cells covering squid bodies, aiding hearing loss research
content:
Scientists have found that squid possess a far greater number of sensory cells than previously known. The animals have cells with bundles of tiny, hairlike protrusions—hair cells—on their heads and arms, similar to those that allow humans to hear.

Researchers at Case Western Reserve University discovered that hundreds more of these hair cells line the entire surface of the squid’s body. This new finding expands the known distribution of hair cells in the species.

The discovery may provide researchers with an unprecedented window into how humans use—and lose—their hearing.
summary: Researchers at Case Western Reserve University discovered that squid have hundreds of hair cells lining the entire surface of their bodies. The finding could provide an unprecedented window into how humans use and lose hearing.
author: Phys.org

title: New imaging technologies offer a clearer view of coral reef change
content:
University of Miami researchers are utilizing new imaging technologies to transform the observation of coral reefs, enabling the measurement of changes that were previously difficult, costly, or time-consuming to document.

The approach involves a range of tools, from drones flying above the waves to cameras positioned just inches from the seafloor. These methods provide a clearer view of reef conditions for scientific analysis.
summary: From a drone flying above the waves to a camera just inches from the seafloor, University of Miami researchers are transforming how scientists observe coral reefs and measure changes that were once difficult, costly or…
author: Phys.org

title: Leucine boosts cellular energy by protecting mitochondrial proteins
content:
Leucine, an essential amino acid, has been shown to enhance cellular energy production by safeguarding key proteins on mitochondria from degradation.  

This discovery uncovers a link between nutrition and metabolism, suggesting that leucine’s protective effect on mitochondrial proteins could inform future strategies for treating metabolic disorders and cancer.
summary: The essential amino acid leucine enhances cellular energy production by preventing the destruction of key proteins on mitochondria. This discovery highlights a new link between nutrition and metabolism, potentially leading to new treatments for metabolic disorders and cancer.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists find an “earthquake gate” as California fault stress hits a 1,000-year high
content:
Scientists have identified a potential “earthquake gate” in Southern California. Researchers report that stress on the San Andreas and San Jacinto faults has risen to some of the highest levels observed in a 1,000‑year simulation.

Because both faults are highly stressed simultaneously, the Cajon Pass junction may be increasingly primed for a rupture that could cross both fault systems. The study does not predict when an earthquake might occur.
summary: Researchers say stress on Southern California’s San Andreas and San Jacinto faults has reached some of the highest levels seen in a 1,000-year simulation. Because both faults are highly stressed at the same time, the Cajon Pass junction may be increasingly primed for a rupture that could cross both systems, although the study does not predict when an earthquake will happen.
author: Science Daily

title: MEGATRON project links JWST galaxy observations to ancient star chemistry
content:
Ultra‑detailed simulations are showing how the first stars lit up the dark Universe and seeded space with elements such as carbon, oxygen, and iron. The new models trace the early stars’ influence on the surrounding medium, revealing the processes that produced the first heavy elements.

The MEGATRON project could bridge observations from the James Webb Space Telescope of the earliest galaxies with the chemical clues preserved in ancient stars today, linking early star formation to the composition of the oldest stellar populations.
summary: Ultra-detailed simulations are showing how the first stars lit up the dark Universe and seeded space with elements such as carbon, oxygen, and iron. The MEGATRON project could bridge JWST observations of the earliest galaxies with chemical clues preserved in ancient stars today.
author: Science Daily

title: Chang’e-6 Lunar Soil Yields New Magnetic Mineral, γ-Fe
content:
Scientists studying Chang’e‑6 lunar soil have identified a previously unknown magnetic mineral in natural Moon samples. The mineral is a form of metallic iron called γ‑Fe.  

The γ‑Fe was found inside tiny impact‑glass particles. At the nanoscale, this iron can preserve a stable magnetic signal. Researchers suggest the mineral could act like a microscopic fossil of the Moon’s long‑lost magnetic field.
summary: Scientists studying Chang’e-6 lunar soil discovered a previously unknown magnetic mineral, a form of metallic iron called γ-Fe. The nanoscale iron, found inside tiny impact‑glass particles, can preserve a stable magnetic signal and may act as a microscopic fossil of the Moon’s long‑lost magnetic field.
author: Science Daily

title: NASA’s Roman Telescope Achieves Precise Pointing, Captures Large Magellanic Cloud Stars
content:
NASA’s Roman Space Telescope has opened its planet‑hunting eye, demonstrating remarkable pointing stability and its first look at the cosmos. The telescope can already stay locked on a target with precision comparable to aiming a laser at a dime from about 150 miles away.

Its coronagraph captured stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud, confirming that the instrument can produce focused images.
summary: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope demonstrated remarkable pointing stability, locking onto targets
author: Science Daily

title: ESA’s Juice uses Earth flyby to slingshot toward Jupiter
content:
ESA’s Juice spacecraft passed Earth on September 28, using the planet’s gravity to alter its trajectory en route to Jupiter. The flyby was executed without significant fuel consumption.

The maneuver changed Juice’s direction by 20 degrees and increased its speed by 3.5 km/s. It also provided scientists with a rare opportunity to test the spacecraft’s instruments on both Earth and the Moon.

The event marks a successful gravity‑assist maneuver for the mission.
summary: ESA’s Juice spacecraft passed Earth on September 28, using the planet’s gravity to alter its trajectory toward Jupiter. The flyby changed its direction by 20 degrees, increased its speed by 3.5 km/s, and allowed scientists to test its instruments on Earth and the Moon.
author: Science Daily

title: Enzyme UBE2N identified as potential defense against worsening fatty liver disease
content: Scientists have identified an enzyme that could serve as a natural defense against the worsening of fatty liver disease, which affects an estimated 100 million Americans. The enzyme, called UBE2N, helps liver cells clear away damaged mitochondria and break down fat. By performing these functions, UBE2N may prevent the inflammation, scarring, and cell damage that can lead to the more dangerous condition known as MASH.
summary: Scientists have identified the enzyme UBE2N, which may act as a natural defense against the worsening of fatty liver disease that affects an estimated 100 million Americans. UBE2N helps liver cells clear damaged mitochondria and break down fat, potentially preventing inflammation, scarring and cell damage associated with MASH.
author: Science Daily

title: UK Bacon Sales Shift to Nitrite‑Free Products Amid Health Concerns
content:
Nitrite‑free bacon sales boom in UK amid fears over curing chemicals

Shoppers are switching from traditional bacon despite little evidence that the alternative is safer.  

Bacon has long been a favourite of carnivores, but growing consumer concern about the health risks posed by nitrites—chemicals used to cure meats—has prompted a shift in buying habits.  

While many experts argue there is no evidence processed meat made without nitrites is safer, retailers have responded to consumer concerns by offering “nitrite‑free” products to meet demand.
summary: Shoppers in the UK are buying nitrite‑free bacon as concerns grow over the health risks of nitrites used in curing meats. Retailers are responding by offering nitrite‑free products, despite experts saying there is no evidence the alternative is safer.
author: Guardian Science

title: Aleph Alpha releases Kolibri, an open-weight LLM for German and English
content:
Kolibri, an open‑weight large language model developed by Aleph Alpha, is designed to operate in both German and English, according to the announcement.

The blog post announcing Kolibri was published at https://tej.As/blog/aleph-alpha-kolibri and generated notable discussion on Hacker News, receiving 262 points and 116 comments (https://news.Ycombinator.Com/item?Id=49943034).

content: Great Question, a Y Combinator Winter 2021 company, announced that it is hiring product engineers based in Canada for remote positions. The job posting is listed on the company’s Y Combinator page. No additional details about the role, compensation, or application process were provided.
summary: Great Question, a Y Combinator Winter 2021 company, is hiring product engineers. The roles are remote and located in Canada.

content:

content:
Meta’s AI agent Muse creates detailed profiles of users’ friends and family, and the tool has been downloaded by millions.  

According to the source, employing Muse to carry out user requests carries privacy costs. Privacy costs are a concern for users of Muse.
summary: Millions have downloaded Meta’s AI agent Muse. Getting it to do your bidding comes with privacy costs.
author: Wired

title: Xreal video glasses revive interest in 3D movies, author says
content:
A The Verge contributor reports that recent advances in video‑glass technology are finally delivering a satisfying 3D movie experience, prompting the writer to purchase 3D Blu‑ray titles in large numbers. The article notes that 3D had long been regarded as one of the biggest tech flops, with earlier theater viewing limited by polarized glasses that reduced resolution and brightness by roughly half.

The piece highlights a demonstration by colleague Cameron Faulkner, who modeled a pair of Xreal glasses, illustrating how modern video glasses overcome the shortcomings of older systems. The writer recalls James Cameron’s Avatar—released more than 15 years ago—as a landmark 3D film that became the highest‑grossing movie worldwide.
summary: The author says they are buying every 3D Blu‑ray they can find because new video glasses make 3D movies enjoyable. They note that earlier polarized theater glasses reduced resolution and brightness, and cite James Cameron’s Avatar as a past high‑grossing 3D film.
author: The Verge

title: OpenAI safety lead David Robinson resigns, warns of broken industry culture
content:
David Robinson, who authored the safety reports accompanying every major model release at OpenAI, resigned from his position this week. In an editorial published in The Atlantic, Robinson announced his departure and began publicly warning about risks associated with the technology he helped develop.

Robinson argues that the problems stem from a fundamentally broken culture within the AI industry, suggesting that merely adding new rules or regulations will not address the deeper issues. He emphasizes that the challenges go beyond surface‑level policy changes.

The full account of Robinson’s resignation and commentary appears in a story on The Verge.
summary: David Robinson, who wrote safety reports for every major OpenAI model release, resigned this week. He is now warning that industry culture is fundamentally broken in an editorial published in The Atlantic.
author: The Verge

title: Splice CEO Kakul Srivastava says AI emails are killing conversations
content:
Splice chief executive Kakul Srivastava says that the rise of AI‑generated emails is “killing conversations,” reflecting her concerns about how automated messaging is affecting communication.  

Srivastava leads Splice, a sample platform that producers use for one‑shot sounds and melodic loops, with tracks from the service appearing in hits such as Lisa’s “Money” and Sabrina Carpenter’s “Espresso.”  Prior to joining Splice, she held executive positions at Flickr, Yahoo, GitHub and Adobe, positioning her at the intersection of Silicon Valley and the creative community.  

Under her leadership, Splice has broadened its reach by acquiring Spitfire Audio and overseeing new initiatives for the company.
summary: Kakul Srivastava, CEO of the music sample platform Splice, believes AI-generated emails are harming conversations. She previously held executive roles at Flickr, Yahoo, GitHub and Adobe and expanded Splice by acquiring Spitfire Audio.
author: The Verge

content:
Spotify billionaire’s body scan startup has come to America

Farooq Abbasi, an investor in Neko Health, spoke with Equity about the company’s future plans. Abbasi discussed the next steps for the hot health‑tech startup, outlining potential growth and strategic directions.

content:
A new compilation identifies the most notable AI agents that can operate within text messaging platforms.  

The list spans a variety of functions, including general‑purpose assistants as well as agents specifically designed for families, travel and work.  

The collection highlights the breadth of capabilities these text‑based AI agents can provide.

title: Vessev unveils electric hydrofoil ferry aiming to reshape boating
content:
Vessev built an electric ferry that almost flies

Vessev has developed an electric hydrofoil ferry that is designed to change how people and cities think about boats. The company hopes its innovative vessel will shift perceptions of maritime transport and inspire new approaches to urban water travel.
summary: Vessev built an electric ferry that almost flies. The company hopes it will change how people and cities think about boats.

title: G7 agrees to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude amid Iran shipping restrictions
content:
The International Energy Agency said that 325 million barrels of emergency oil have been released, with an additional 75 million barrels slated for release.

G7 leaders agreed on Friday to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude after U.S. pressure on Europe, noting that supplies have been squeezed by Iran’s restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
summary: G7 leaders agreed on Friday to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude. The release was prompted by US pressure on Europe and Iran's restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
author: Euronews

title: Tens of thousands protest in Madrid after lawmakers reject tenant‑protection measures
content:
Tens of thousands of protesters marched in Madrid and other Spanish cities on Saturday, calling for affordable housing. The demonstrations were driven by anger over lawmakers’ narrow rejection of a set of measures put forward by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s government.

The rejected proposals were intended to strengthen protection for tenants, prompting demonstrators to demand stronger housing relief.
summary: Tens of thousands of protesters marched in Madrid and other Spanish cities on Saturday demanding affordable housing. The demonstrations were sparked by lawmakers narrowly rejecting measures put forward by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s government to strengthen protection for tenants.
author: France 24

title: Houthis say Saudi forces carried out 26 strikes on Sanaa amid loud blasts
content:
Loud blasts rocked Sanaa on Saturday, prompting Houthi rebels to accuse Saudi forces of launching 26 strikes on the Yemeni capital. The rebels said the explosions followed a series of attacks that they claim targeted the city, which is under the control of the Iran‑backed group.

In Saudi Arabia, observers reported flames and a large plume of smoke rising from an oil giant Aramco facility located south of the kingdom’s capital, Riyadh. The incident was noted as part of the broader conflict between the Saudi‑backed coalition and the Houthi movement.

The accusations and the reported Saudi facility fire were both reported on Saturday.
summary: Houthi rebels accused Saudi forces of launching 26 strikes on Sanaa on Saturday after loud explosions rocked the Yemeni capital, which they control. Flames and a large plume of smoke were seen rising from an Aramco facility south of Riyadh in Saudi Arabia.
author: France 24

title: France to share defence files with Italy in probe of 1980 Ustica jet crash
content:
France has agreed to share defence documents with the Italian judiciary, a move that has sparked hopes of a breakthrough in investigations into the 1980 crash of a passenger jet near the island of Ustica. The crash, which killed 81 people, has long been a subject of controversy, and a former Italian president has claimed that the aircraft was mistakenly shot down by a French fighter jet.

Despite the new access to French files, sceptics warn that the documents are unlikely to shed light on one of Italy’s most enduring mysteries or identify a culprit. The Italian authorities will now review the material, but no definitive outcome has been announced.
summary: France has decided to share defence documents with the Italian judiciary, sparking hopes of a breakthrough in the investigation of the 1980 passenger jet crash near the island of Ustica. Sceptics note that the files may not illuminate the long‑standing mystery or identify a responsible party, despite a former Italian president’s claim that a French fighter jet mistakenly shot down the aircraft.
author: France 24

title: Eritrea Cuts Ties with Ethiopia, Heightening War Fear in Horn of Africa
content:
The Tigray conflict has expanded beyond a domestic dispute, raising concerns across the Horn of Africa. After Eritrea severed diplomatic ties with Ethiopia, tensions have escalated as Ethiopia, Eritrea, and Egypt exchange accusations.

In response, the African Union has called for restraint amid the growing uncertainty. The situation prompts questions about whether the region is moving toward a broader crisis.
summary: The Tigray conflict has expanded beyond domestic borders as Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt trade accusations. The African Union (AU) urges restraint amid concerns the Horn of Africa may face a wider regional crisis.
author: DW World

title: Kenyan survivors challenge UK military over alleged decades of abuse and immunity
content: Kenyan survivors are challenging the United Kingdom’s military over decades of alleged abuses. The survivors contend that the UK forces have been protected by legal immunity that has shielded them from accountability. Their effort seeks to confront both the historic allegations and the legal safeguards that have prevented redress. The case underscores a broader dispute over responsibility and justice for the alleged misconduct.
summary: Kenyan survivors are challenging the UK military over alleged abuses that span decades. They argue that the military’s legal immunity has protected it from accountability.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Israel election sees Arab leader forced to withdraw, far‑right candidates cleared
content:
In the latest Israeli election cycle, a Palestinian Israeli leader was compelled to withdraw his candidacy, while far‑right Israeli leaders were permitted to remain on the ballot.  

The contrasting treatment has been described as a double standard, with the forced exit of the Palestinian candidate standing in stark contrast to the clearance of right‑wing contenders.  

The episode has drawn attention to perceived disparities in how candidates are handled in the polls.
summary: A Palestinian Israeli leader was forced to withdraw his candidacy. Far‑right Israeli leaders were allowed to run in the polls.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Brazil 2026 presidential race tight between incumbent Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro
content:
Brazil’s 2026 presidential election is shaping up as a close contest, with polls indicating a tight race between incumbent Lula and right‑wing rival Flavio Bolsonaro.  

Voter concerns over crime and the economy are central to the campaign, underscoring the issues driving the competition between the two candidates.
summary: Polls show a tight race between incumbent Lula and right‑wing rival Flavio Bolsonaro. The contest is occurring amid concerns over crime and the economy.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Tens of thousands protest in Spain after parliament rejects two housing decrees
content:
Tens of thousands of people took to the streets in Spain after parliament struck down two affordable‑housing decrees, according to reports.  

The latest demonstrations have deepened a crisis that has persisted for several days, following the legislative rejection of the housing measures.
summary: Tens of thousands of people demonstrated in Spain. The demonstrations deepened a days‑long crisis after parliament struck down two affordable housing decrees.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Democrats upbeat in final US midterm month as Republicans spend to curb losses
content:
‘Bordering on angry’: The state of play as US midterms enter final month

As the United States midterm elections move into their final month, the political landscape is described as “bordering on angry.” The title underscores the heightened tension surrounding the closing weeks of the contests.

Democrats are entering the stretch with a surprisingly positive outlook, while Republican campaign funds are being deployed in an effort to stem damage to their party’s prospects.
summary: Democrats have entered the final stretch of the US midterms with a surprisingly positive outlook. Republican money is being deployed in an effort to stem damage.

title: Brazil accuses US of election interference amid Lula‑da‑Silva and Bolsonaro clash over sovereignty
content:
Brazil is preparing to vote for its next president, and the campaign has been marked by accusations that the United States is interfering in the election.  

The contest pits former president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva against former president Jair Bolsonaro, with both candidates sparring over issues of sovereignty, security and Brazil’s ties with Washington.  

The dispute over foreign influence has led Brazilian officials to publicly accuse the United States of meddling in the electoral process.
summary: Brazil has accused the United States of interfering in its upcoming presidential election. The accusation comes as Lula da Silva and Bolsonaro clash over sovereignty, security and ties with Washington.
author: BBC World

content:
Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe 2026: horse‑by‑horse guide to all the runners

The 2026 edition of the Prix de l’Arc de Triomphe is shaping up to feature a rare repeat success, with Daryz well fancied to contend. In Paris, O’Brien Jr and Sr will go head‑to‑head, adding intrigue to the field.

title: India defeat Pakistan by 19 runs to win Asian Games cricket gold in Japan
content:
India defeated arch‑rivals Pakistan by 19 runs to win the Asian Games men’s Twenty20 cricket gold medal in Nagoya, Japan. India posted 211 for 6 in 20 overs, while Pakistan finished on 192 for 6.

Key performances included Abhishek Sharma’s 61 and Tilak Varma’s unbeaten 51 for India, and Hasan Nawaz’s 96 for Pakistan. The match, played on a converted baseball field, drew a small but raucous crowd and was watched by millions of fans on television.

The captains of both sides declined the customary pre‑match handshakes, a gesture reflecting the political tensions between the two nations. After the victory, Indian players paraded their national flag around the ground.
summary: India posted 211‑6 and beat Pakistan, which scored 192‑6, by 19 runs in the Asian Games T20 final in Nagoya, Japan. The captains refused the traditional pre‑match handshakes and Indian players later paraded their national flag around the ground.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Verstappen grabs first pole of year at Bahrain GP in Malaysia as Russell risks points
content:
Max Verstappen secured his first pole position of the year at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, taking the top spot for Red Bull. Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton started second on the front row, Kimi Antonelli finished fourth, and George Russell was down in eighth.

The most consequential story for the Formula One World Championship is the widening gap between title leader Kimi Antonelli and his Mercedes teammate George Russell. Russell, who has been floundering in Sepang, now faces the risk of losing additional points that he cannot afford while chasing Antonelli.

content:

content:
A decade‑long experiment designed to explore the ocean’s “deep reefs” has yielded its first results. Scientists placed artificial structures on the seafloor at depths of up to 100 meters and left them in place for ten years.

After a ten‑year interval, the researchers recovered the structures and documented what had developed on and around them. The retrieval provides new observations that will help scientists better understand the biology and dynamics of deep‑water reef habitats.
summary: Scientists left structures up to 100 meters under the surface as part of a decade‑long experiment. They retrieved the structures ten years later and reported what they found.

content:

content:

content:

content:
UAE officials said a FlyDubai co‑pilot attacked the aircraft’s captain with an axe, describing the act as “terrorist.” The assault occurred on a flight bound for Tel‑Aviv and nearly caused a crash.

The co‑pilot, identified as Omani national Hamam al‑Hammami, had previously been barred from flying by Oman after authorities expressed concerns that he showed signs of extremist views.

The incident added to the strain on the already hard‑hit regional travel industry, pushing it further into crisis.

content:

content:
Russia’s air forces hit Kyiv’s Northern Bridge across the Dnipro River, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Saturday, marking another escalation in attacks on the capital’s infrastructure.

content:
Ethiopia’s Tigray rebels abandoned their regional capital of Mekkele in the north of the country on Saturday, local reports said.

The Tigray People’s Liberation Front has been fighting against federal forces and pro‑government militias since September 23, and has launched attacks into neighbouring states. The advance of pro‑government forces has raised fears of an all‑out civil war similar to that of 2020‑2022.

content:
The Stade de France was filled to capacity as Zinedine Zidane made his home debut as the new manager of the French national team. His first match in charge came against Italy, the side against which he ended his playing career in 2006.

content:

title: Brazil's tight presidential race tests pro‑Trump Latin American bloc
content:
Brazil’s upcoming presidential election is a tight race, with a Sunday poll showing the left‑wing incumbent Lula facing the son of a former far‑right president who was convicted of staging a coup.  The contest has also raised concerns about the influence of Brazil’s patron saint, as reflected in the headline “No one disrespects Our Lady,” which highlights fears that the saint’s grip on the country could shape the election outcome.

Shortly after a controversial speech to the United Nations General Assembly in September, former President Donald Trump convened a dozen Latin American leaders who share his right‑wing views.  Trump boasted that every right‑wing candidate he has endorsed has won, noting that all seven presidential elections held in the region since he began his second term have gone to right‑wing candidates.  He delivered these remarks in New York before the Shield of the Americas, an anti‑drug cartel coalition of 15 right‑ or far‑right‑governed countries.

The poll and Trump’s statements underscore the test facing the growing pro‑Trump bloc in Latin America as Brazil’s election approaches.

content:

Allegations that the son of warlord Khalifa Haftar oversaw a “terror cell” that launched drone attacks on fuel storage facilities and power stations in western Libya have upended the GNU’s plans to continue cooperating with Haftar on a national unification strategy.  

Saddam Haftar, the deputy commander of the so‑called Libyan National Army (LNA), has increasingly been viewed by the United States as a key figure in its plans to unify Libyan security, judicial and political institutions.

title: Jonathan Liew urges fan ownership and restitution over retribution for Manchester City
content:
Following the revelation that Manchester City has been found guilty of all financial charges by the Premier League, Jonathan Liew argues that the appropriate response should prioritize restitution over retribution, ultimately suggesting the club be handed over to its fans. Liew notes that while there are no real precedents and emotions remain raw, the current situation offers an opportunity for positive change through a shift in ownership models.

The article highlights the widespread and often humorous reactions to the verdict, describing a "great and cathartic silliness" that has emerged in the days since the news broke. Liew lists various satirical punishments proposed by the public, including a 17-year transfer embargo, forcing Ferran Soriano to drive a parade bus backwards through Manchester for every major trophy won, and banning the "Poznan" celebration or requiring fans to perform it facing forwards.

The piece also references specific social media trolling from brands, such as Sainsbury’s posting an image of "114 unexpected items in the bagging area" and Domino’s Pizza claiming to have "irrefutable evidence that pineapple is the best pizza topping." Liew concludes that while these reactions are prevalent, the long-term solution lies in altering how football clubs are owned and operated.
summary: Jonathan Liew argues that changing ownership models to hand Manchester City to the fans is a better path than retributive punishment. He notes that while emotions are raw and precedents are lacking, good can come from the situation if these changes occur.
